gloss.intro: The words developers (and the 🤖 teams) use, in plain English.
gloss.switch.help: 💡 Words with a dotted underline get a plain explanation when you hover over them.
gloss.backlog.text: 💡 The waiting list of ideas and work not planned in yet, with the most important at the top. Nothing there gets worked on until it moves to To do.
gloss.sprint.text: 🏃 A short, fixed stretch of work (often one or two weeks, never more than a month) with a goal and an agreed set of cards to finish.
gloss.standup.text: 📣 A quick daily check-in: what each team member did, what they do next, and what is stopping them. In Scrum it is called the daily scrum.
gloss.bug.text: 🐞 Something that doesn’t work the way it should.
gloss.test.text: 🧪 A check that something works the way it should. Some tests the computer runs by itself every time the code changes; others are you trying a finished card before you accept it.
gloss.commit.text: 📸 A saved snapshot of the code, with a short note of what changed. You can always go back to one.
gloss.push.text: ⬆️ Sending your saved snapshots (commits) from this computer to the shared copy online, such as GitHub, so they are backed up and others can get them.
gloss.branch.text: 🌿 A separate line of work in the code, so changes can be made without touching the main version.
gloss.merge.text: 🔀 Joining the changes from one branch into another, usually back into the main version.
gloss.repo.text: 🗂️ The project’s folder of code with its full history of commits. It can live on your computer, on GitHub, or both.
gloss.refactor.text: 🧹 Tidying the code without changing what it does: smaller files, clearer names, less repetition.
gloss.deploy.text: 🚀 Copying a new version of the software onto the computers that run it, such as a test copy or the live service.
gloss.kanban.text: 📋 A way of working where cards move across a board’s columns (like To do, In progress, Done) and the team limits how much is in progress at once, so work keeps flowing.
gloss.wip.text: 🚧 WIP is short for work in progress. A WIP limit is the most cards a column should hold at once, so the team finishes things before starting more.
gloss.pr.text: 🙏 Asking for a branch’s changes to be checked and merged into the main version. Some sites call it a merge request.
gloss.hook.text: 🪝 A small command that runs by itself at a set moment, for example when an AI session starts, so the team hears your comments.
gloss.token.text: 🪙 The small pieces of text an AI reads and writes, about three quarters of a word each. AI use is counted in tokens, so fewer tokens leave more of your plan.
gloss.agent.text: 🤖 An AI that works on a task by itself: reads the code, makes changes, runs checks and reports back. Its work still gets checked.

gloss.title: 📖 Words explained 💡
gloss.about: 📖 Free training in plain language: every word you meet from a first 💡 to a service people rely on 🛎️, with Agile 🔁, building 🛠️, keeping it safe 🔒 and working with 🤖 along the way.
gloss.about.noai: 📖 Free training in plain language: every word you meet from a first 💡 to a service people rely on 🛎️, with Agile 🔁, building 🛠️ and keeping it safe 🔒 along the way.
gloss.g.team: 🤝 Working as a team (and with AI 🤖)
gloss.card.text: 🃏 One piece of work: a job, a 🐞 or a 💡. It moves across the columns until it is done ✅.
gloss.project.text: 📁 A board for one thing you want to get done, like an app 📱, a garden shed 🏡 or a trip ✈️. It holds the 🃏 cards.
gloss.forteam.text: 👥 The column for cards that are the team's turn again, for example after you answered their ❓ or asked for a change.
gloss.lead.text: 🧭 The 🤖 helper in charge of a project. It picks up your 🃏 cards, shares out the work, and asks you when it needs you.
gloss.agentprog.text: 🖥️ The 🤖 program on your computer, like Claude Code, that the board starts when there is work for your helpers.
gloss.dispatcher.text: 🚦 The part of the board that reads a new 🃏 or 💬 and decides who picks it up. Simple rules first, a small 🤖 only when unsure.
gloss.space.text: 🪐 A group of projects that belong together, like a 📁 for boards. 🪐 marks one.
gloss.playground.text: 🛝 A ready-made project 📦 for a friend to try AI-gile in, with an invite code 🎟️ to send them.
gloss.hyperfocus.text: 🎯 Shows only one project and your messages, so nothing else pulls at you. The teams carry on as normal.
gloss.qa.text: ✅ Short for quality assurance: everything done to make sure work is right before it goes live. In AI-gile that means the automatic checks: when QA is red 🔴, something failed, and it can’t go live until that is fixed.
gloss.release.text: A named bundle of finished work that goes live together, with short notes on what changed. 🚀 Releases writes the notes from the done cards. 📦
gloss.rollback.text: ⏪ Going back to the last version that worked when a new one causes trouble. In AI-gile, Roll back gathers the undo steps written on each change into one checklist.
gloss.live.text: The real version that people use, as opposed to a copy for trying things out. Developers also call it production. 🌍
gloss.change.text: A planned change to something people rely on, written down first: what, why, the risk, when, and how to undo it. Start one with 🔀 Raise a change. 🔀
gloss.risk.text: Something that could go wrong, scored on how likely and how bad it would be. ⚠️ Risks keeps them in one list, highest score first, each with a date to look again. ⚠️
gloss.chgwin.text: The times when changes may go live, such as a quiet Tuesday evening. Outside a window a change card can’t be finished, unless it is an emergency. 🪟
gloss.gonogo.text: 🚦 A last check just before a change goes live: each person who has to approve says Go or No go. It only goes ahead when everyone says Go.
gloss.approval.text: Waiting for a yes before work starts. A card a friend raises, or a change, waits in ✅ Approvals until you approve or decline it. ✅
gloss.quiettime.text: 🤫 A stretch of time, like during a live stream, a demo or overnight, when nothing goes live. The teams keep working and testing, but going live waits until it ends. Elsewhere it is called a change freeze.
gloss.service.text: Something you built that people rely on, like a website 🌐 or an app 📱, looked after so it keeps working. Tick “This project is a service” and say what it offers, who uses it and who is on call. 🛎️
gloss.uptime.text: An automatic check, every few minutes, that your service still answers. If it fails several times in a row, AI-gile opens an incident card by itself. 💓
gloss.statuspage.text: A public page that shows whether a service is working (🟢, 🟠 or 🔴) with the latest update, so the people who use it can check instead of asking. 🚥
gloss.incident.text: 🔥 Something that is broken or not working properly for the people using it right now, like the website being down or very slow. A 🔥 incident card jumps the queue: getting it working again comes first.
gloss.major.text: A big incident: many people affected, or money 💰 or data 📊 at risk. One button puts every team on it (swarm), wakes ⏰ whoever is on call and asks for a status update every 30 minutes ⏱️. 🚨
gloss.oncall.text: Being the one who answers when something breaks, even at night 🌙 🌙. Each service has an on-call team member who is woken first for its incidents. 📟
gloss.replyby.text: How long a card may wait for a first answer, for example an hour for an incident. After that it gets a red clock ⏰, so nothing is quietly forgotten. Also called a response target. ⏰
gloss.postmortem.text: A short look back after an incident: what happened, what helped and what to change, without blaming anyone 🙅. An incident can’t be closed without one. 🔍
gloss.problem.text: The hidden cause behind one or more incidents. A 🧩 problem card groups incidents that keep coming back, so the cause is found and fixed for good. 🧩
gloss.rootcause.text: The real reason something broke, not just what you saw going wrong. Fix the root cause and the incident stops coming back. 🌱
gloss.workaround.text: A way to keep things working until the real fix is ready, like restarting something when it gets stuck. It is written on the problem card so nobody has to work it out again. 🩹
gloss.knownerror.text: 🧩 A problem whose cause is understood but isn’t fixed yet, usually with a workaround written down. 🧩 Known errors lists them, so everyone uses the workaround instead of digging again.
gloss.runbook.text: Step-by-step instructions for fixing a known kind of trouble, so it is done the same way, quickly, every time. After a big incident the team can propose one for you to OK. 📘
gloss.backup.text: A saved copy of your data from earlier, to fall back on if something is lost or damaged. AI-gile makes a backup of your boards every day 📅. 💾
gloss.restore.text: Putting data back from a backup. A backup only really counts once you know it can be restored 🔴, so it is worth trying now and then. ♻️
gloss.dod.text: The team’s short checklist of what “finished” means, like tested and explained, before a card is handed to you. Its twin, the Definition of Ready, says when a card is clear enough to start. 🏁
gloss.testpile.text: The finished cards waiting for you to try, one after another. Accept one or send it back with a note, and the next one comes up. 🗂️
gloss.retro.text: 🪞 A regular look back at how the team works, to agree on one or two things to do better next time. Short for retrospective. In AI-gile a retro suggests a change to the team’s ways of working, and you say Go or Not yet.
gloss.peerreview.text: 👀 A second pair of eyes: someone other than the author checks the work before it reaches you, so fewer mistakes get through. In AI-gile another 🤖 checks each card.
gloss.swarm.text: 🐝 All hands on deck: many people drop other work to fix one urgent thing together until it is sorted. In AI-gile every team helps on one project, and other projects wait meanwhile.
gloss.scrummaster.text: 🧑‍🏫 In Scrum, the person who helps the team work well: clears what blocks them, keeps meetings on track and coaches good habits, without bossing anyone. In AI-gile the Lead Scrum Master spots stuck cards, nudges the teams and reminds you of what is waiting, across every project.
gloss.scrummaster.text.noai: 🧑‍🏫 In Scrum, the person who helps the team work well: clears what blocks them, keeps meetings on track and coaches good habits, without bossing anyone. Without 🤖, AI-gile’s version spots stuck cards and works with fixed commands, like sorting To do.
gloss.discovery.text: 🔎 The early stage of finding out which problem is worth solving and for whom, before anything gets built.
gloss.problemstmt.text: 📝 One or two sentences saying who has a problem, what it is and why it matters, so everyone aims at the same 🎯.
gloss.user.text: 🧑 A person who uses what you build. Their needs are what the work is for.
gloss.stakeholder.text: 🤝 Anyone who cares how the work turns out or is affected by it, like the people paying for it 💰, using it or supporting it.
gloss.persona.text: 🎭 A made-up but realistic person who stands for one kind of user, so the team can ask “would Sam find this easy?”
gloss.userresearch.text: 👂 Talking to and watching real people to learn what they need, rather than guessing 🤷.
gloss.journey.text: 🗺️ The steps a person takes to get something done, from first hearing about it to finishing, also outside your product. Drawing it out shows where they get stuck.
gloss.painpoint.text: 😣 Something that annoys or slows people down today. Good products take pain points away.
gloss.assumption.text: 🤔 Something you believe but haven’t checked yet. Writing assumptions down shows what to test first.
gloss.hypothesis.text: 🔮 A best guess you plan to check, with what you expect to happen, like “people will sign up if the first month is free”.
gloss.experiment.text: 🧪 A small planned test to learn whether an idea works, before betting a lot on it.
gloss.poc.text: ⚡ A quick rough try to see if an idea can work at all. It is usually thrown away 🗑️ once you have the answer.
gloss.prototype.text: 🧸 An early model of the product, often clickable pictures, to try the idea on people before building it properly.
gloss.wireframe.text: ✏️ A simple sketch of a screen showing where things go, without colours or real content.
gloss.mockup.text: 🖼️ A detailed picture of how a screen will look, with real colours 🎨 and text, but nothing works yet.
gloss.bizcase.text: 💼 The reasons for doing a project: what it costs, what it brings in or saves, and the risks ⚠️.
gloss.feasibility.text: 🏗️ Whether something can really be built and looked after with the time ⏱️, money 💰 and skills you have.
gloss.outcome.text: 🌱 The change you want for people, like fewer missed appointments. It matters more than how much you build.
gloss.output.text: 📦 Something the team makes, like a new screen or a report. Making it doesn’t automatically mean it helps anyone.
gloss.successmetric.text: 📏 A number that tells you whether the work did what it was for, like more people finishing their order.
gloss.kpi.text: 📊 An important number you watch to see if things are going well, like sign-ups per week.
gloss.okr.text: 🎯 A way of setting goals: the objective says what you want, and a few key results are the numbers that show you got there.
gloss.product.text: 🎁 The thing being built and looked after for its users, such as an app 📱, a website 🌐 or a tool 🔧.
gloss.vision.text: 🔭 A short statement of who the product helps and where it is heading in the long run.
gloss.po.text: 👑 The person who decides what gets built and in what order, so the team always works on what matters most. In AI-gile that is you.
gloss.pm.text: 🧭 The person who looks after a product’s direction: which problems it solves, for whom and why. PM can also mean project manager, so check which.
gloss.projmgr.text: 📆 The person who keeps a project on time ⏱️ and on budget 💰, tracking who does what and by when.
gloss.roadmap.text: 🛣️ A rough plan of what is coming over the next months, in order. It shows direction, not exact dates, and changes as you learn.
gloss.milestone.text: 🚩 A point in a project worth marking, like “first version live” or “100 users”.
gloss.mvp.text: 🌱 The smallest version of a product that is still useful to real people, so you can learn from them early.
gloss.requirement.text: 📋 Something the finished product must do or be.
gloss.scope.text: 🔲 What is included in the work and, just as important, what is not.
gloss.scopecreep.text: 🐛 When more and more gets added to the work bit by bit, without anyone agreeing on the extra time ⏱️ or cost 💰, so it never quite finishes.
gloss.feature.text: ✨ One thing the product can do for people, like “reset your password”.
gloss.epic.text: 🏔️ A big piece of work, too large for one go, so it is split into smaller 🃏 cards.
gloss.story.text: 📖 A small piece of work written from the user’s side: “As a shopper, I want to save my basket, so I can finish later.” It starts a conversation about what to build.
gloss.ac.text: ✅ The checks one card must pass to count as done, agreed before work starts, like “the basket is still there after I log out and back in”.
gloss.task.text: 🔨 A single job to be done, often one small step of a bigger story.
gloss.ticket.text: 🎫 Another word for a card: one piece of work or one request, tracked from start to finish.
gloss.priority.text: 🔝 How important or urgent something is compared with everything else, so the most important work goes first.
gloss.prioritise.text: 🥇 Putting work in order of importance. A common way is MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won’t have this time.
gloss.estimate.text: 🤏 A best guess at how big or how long a piece of work is. It is a guess, not a promise 🤞.
gloss.storypoints.text: 🔢 A way of guessing the size of work by comparing cards with each other (“about twice as big as that one”) rather than in hours. They aren’t for comparing teams.
gloss.tshirt.text: 👕 Guessing the size of work as S, M, L or XL. Quick and good enough for early planning.
gloss.poker.text: 🃏 A game for estimating: everyone shows a size card at the same time, then the highest and lowest explain why.
gloss.dependency.text: 🔗 When one piece of work can’t start or finish until another one does.
gloss.blocker.text: 🚧 Anything stopping work from moving forward right now, like a missing answer or a broken tool.
gloss.deadline.text: ⏰ The date something must be finished by.
gloss.deliverable.text: 📦 Something concrete the work produces and hands over, like a working page or a report.
gloss.forecast.text: 🌤️ A prediction of what is likely to happen, like when the work will be done, based on what you know so far.
gloss.metric.text: 📈 Anything you measure and track over time, like page visits or how long a fix takes.
gloss.feedback.text: 💬 What people tell you about your work, good 👍 and bad 👎. Getting it early and often is the heart of Agile.
gloss.agile.text: 🔁 A way of working in small steps: build a little, show real results often, learn from what people say and change the plan as you go, instead of planning everything up front.
gloss.manifesto.text: 📜 A short statement written in 2001 by software makers. It puts people, working results, close work with customers and responding to change ahead of heavy plans and paperwork.
gloss.waterfall.text: 🌊 The older way of working: plan everything, then build it all, then test it all, one stage after another. Changes late on are hard and costly 💰.
gloss.iteration.text: 🔄 One round of building something, checking it and improving it. Agile work is a chain of these, and a 🏃 sprint is one kind.
gloss.increment.text: 🧩 A new working piece added to the product in a sprint or round of work, which fits with what was already there.
gloss.scrum.text: 🏉 A popular Agile way of working: a small team works in short sprints towards a goal, with set roles and a few regular meetings to plan, check and improve.
gloss.scrumteam.text: 👥 The small group that does the work in Scrum: a product owner, a Scrum Master and the developers.
gloss.ceremonies.text: 🎪 The regular meetings in Scrum: sprint planning, the daily scrum, the sprint review and the retro. Many people call them ceremonies.
gloss.sprintplan.text: 🗓️ The meeting at the start of a sprint where the team agrees why the sprint matters, which cards to take on and how to start.
gloss.sprintgoal.text: 🎯 One sentence saying what a sprint is for. Small tasks can change along the way, as long as the goal is met.
gloss.sprintbacklog.text: 🗃️ The cards picked for the current sprint, with the team’s plan for doing them.
gloss.productbacklog.text: 🗃️ The full ordered list of everything that might be built for the product, most important at the top. It keeps changing as you learn.
gloss.productgoal.text: 🏁 The bigger result the product is working towards, which helps the team choose what to do next.
gloss.refinement.text: 🧹 Regularly going through the backlog to tidy, split, order and add detail to cards, so they are ready to pick up. Also called backlog grooming.
gloss.sprintreview.text: 👀 A meeting at the end of a sprint where the team shows what it finished and hears what people think, to decide what comes next.
gloss.demo.text: 🎬 Showing finished work working, live, to the people who asked for it.
gloss.timebox.text: ⏳ A fixed amount of time for something. When it runs out you stop, even if not everything is done.
gloss.velocity.text: 🚀 How much work a team usually finishes in a sprint, used to plan how much to take on next time. It isn’t a score for how hard people work.
gloss.capacity.text: 🪣 How much work the team can take on in a period, after holidays 🏖️ and other jobs.
gloss.burndown.text: 📉 A chart of the work left in a sprint going down day by day. If the line stays flat, something is stuck.
gloss.burnup.text: 📈 A chart of finished work going up over time, next to the total planned, so you can see when you will get there.
gloss.kanbanboard.text: 📋 The board itself: a column for each stage of the work, with cards moving across.
gloss.pullsys.text: 🧲 A way of working where new work only starts when someone has room to take it on, rather than being pushed onto a full plate.
gloss.flow.text: 🌊 How smoothly work moves across the board. Good flow means cards keep moving rather than piling up.
gloss.leadtime.text: ⏱️ How long it takes from someone asking for something to it being finished.
gloss.cycletime.text: ⏲️ How long a card takes from when work really starts on it to when it is finished.
gloss.throughput.text: 🏭 How many cards get finished in a week, or in any set time.
gloss.bottleneck.text: 🍾 The one stage where work piles up and slows everything behind it, like the narrow neck of a bottle.
gloss.swimlane.text: 🏊 A row across the board that groups cards of one kind, such as urgent work or one team’s cards.
gloss.lean.text: 🌿 A way of working that cuts out waste (anything that doesn’t help the customer) and keeps work flowing.
gloss.waste.text: 🗑️ In Lean, anything that takes effort but doesn’t help the customer, like waiting, rework or building things nobody uses.
gloss.kaizen.text: 🌱 Getting a little better all the time through small regular changes, then checking they helped. Retros are one way to do it. Also called kaizen.
gloss.selforg.text: 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 A team that decides for itself how to do the work, rather than being told step by step.
gloss.crossfunc.text: 🧰 A team that has all the skills it needs to finish the work itself, like design 🎨, building 🏗️ and testing 🧪.
gloss.spike.text: 🔦 A short, timeboxed bit of research to answer a question before committing to the real work.
gloss.rework.text: 🔁 Doing work again because it wasn’t right the first time.
gloss.safe.text: 🏢 Ways of using Agile across many teams in a big organisation. SAFe (the Scaled Agile Framework) is one well known example.
gloss.code.text: 💻 The written instructions that tell a computer what to do. Also called source code.
gloss.proglang.text: 🔤 A language for writing code, such as JavaScript, Python or Java. Different ones suit different jobs.
gloss.developer.text: 🧑‍💻 Someone who writes and changes code. Also called a programmer or software engineer.
gloss.software.text: 💿 Programs that run on computers and phones, as opposed to the machines themselves (the hardware).
gloss.app.text: 📱 Short for application: a program people use to get something done, on a phone, a computer or in a web browser.
gloss.webapp.text: 🌐 An app that runs in a web browser, so there is nothing to install.
gloss.frontend.text: 🖱️ The part of an app you see and click on: the screens, buttons and words, often in your browser.
gloss.backend.text: ⚙️ The behind-the-scenes part of an app that keeps the data and does the work when you click something, like checking your password 🔑.
gloss.fullstack.text: 🥞 Working on both the front end and the back end.
gloss.ui.text: 🖼️ What a person sees and uses on screen: layout, buttons, menus and text.
gloss.ux.text: 😊 How it feels to use something: easy, clear and pleasant, or confusing and slow 😵.
gloss.accessibility.text: ♿ Making things usable by everyone, including people who can’t see well, can’t use a mouse or use a screen reader.
gloss.responsive.text: 📱💻 Making pages fit and work well on any screen size, from a phone to a big monitor.
gloss.designsys.text: 🎨 A shared kit of colours, fonts, buttons and rules, so every screen looks and behaves the same way.
gloss.architecture.text: 🏛️ The overall shape of a system: what the main parts are and how they talk to each other.
gloss.database.text: 🗄️ An organised store of information, like a very powerful spreadsheet 📊 that the app can read and change.
gloss.schema.text: 📐 The layout of a database: which tables of information it has and what goes in each.
gloss.sql.text: 🔍 Short for structured query language: the language used to ask many databases for information or to change it.
gloss.data.text: 💾 Information kept by a computer, like names, orders or settings.
gloss.server.text: 🖥️ A computer that is always on and answers requests from other computers, like sending a web page when you visit it.
gloss.client.text: 🙋 The side that asks for something, usually your browser or app, talking to a server. In business it also just means a customer.
gloss.api.text: 🔌 Short for application programming interface: a set menu of requests one program can make to another, like asking a weather service for today’s forecast 🌦️.
gloss.endpoint.text: 📍 One item on an API’s menu: a web address a program can call to get or send something.
gloss.integration.text: 🔗 Connecting two systems so they work together, like your shop sending orders to your accounts software.
gloss.webhook.text: 🪝 A message one system sends to another by itself the moment something happens, like “payment received”.
gloss.library.text: 📚 Ready-made code someone else wrote that you can reuse instead of writing it yourself.
gloss.framework.text: 🏠 A ready-made structure for building an app that decides much of how the code is laid out, like a house frame you fill in.
gloss.sdk.text: 🧰 A box of tools, code and examples for building software for one platform or service.
gloss.softdep.text: 🔗 A library or tool your code needs to work. Keeping them up to date matters for safety 🔒.
gloss.package.text: 📦 A bundle of ready-made code you can install and use in a project.
gloss.pkgmgr.text: 🚚 A tool that fetches and updates the packages your code depends on. npm is a common one.
gloss.git.text: 🌳 The most widely used tool for keeping the history of code changes, as commits and branches.
gloss.github.text: 🐙 A website that keeps Git repos online, so teams can share code, review changes and track work.
gloss.vcs.text: 🕰️ Keeping a full history of every change to the files, so you can see who changed what and go back if needed. Git does this.
gloss.clone.text: 🐑 Making your own full copy of a repo, with its history, on your computer.
gloss.pull.text: ⬇️ Fetching the latest commits from the shared copy (like GitHub) onto your computer. The opposite of push.
gloss.mainbranch.text: 🌳 The official version of the code that everyone works from, often called main or master.
gloss.conflict.text: 💥 When two changes touch the same lines in different ways, so the computer can’t join them and a person has to choose.
gloss.diff.text: 🔀 A view showing exactly what changed between two versions: lines added ➕ and lines taken away ➖.
gloss.fork.text: 🍴 Your own copy of someone else’s repo, which you can change without affecting theirs.
gloss.script.text: 📜 A short program that does one job by itself, like tidying files or starting the app.
gloss.build.text: 🏗️ Turning the code into something ready to run, or the ready-to-run result itself.
gloss.compile.text: ⚙️ Translating code people wrote into a form the computer can run directly.
gloss.cli.text: ⌨️ A text window where you type instructions for the computer instead of clicking. Also called the terminal.
gloss.config.text: 🎛️ The settings that control how software behaves, kept apart from the code so they are easy to change.
gloss.envvar.text: 🔑 A setting handed to a program when it starts, often used for addresses or passwords so they aren’t written into the code.
gloss.debugging.text: 🔍🐞 Hunting down why something isn’t working, and fixing it.
gloss.pairing.text: 👯 Two people (or a person and an 🤖) working on the same code together, one typing and one checking.
gloss.docs.text: 📚 Written explanations of how something works or how to use it.
gloss.readme.text: 📄 The first file to read in a repo: what the project is and how to get it running.
gloss.legacy.text: 🦖 An older system still in use that is hard to change, often because few people still understand it.
gloss.techdebt.text: 💳 Shortcuts that save time now but make later changes slower, like a loan that builds up interest. Refactoring pays it down.
gloss.autotest.text: 🤖 A check the computer runs by itself every time the code changes, to catch mistakes early.
gloss.manualtest.text: 🖐️ A person trying the work by hand to see if it behaves as it should.
gloss.unittest.text: 🔬 A small automatic check of one tiny piece of code on its own.
gloss.integtest.text: 🧩 A check that several parts work properly together, not just one at a time.
gloss.endtoend.text: 🛒 A test that acts like a real user from start to finish, such as signing up, buying and paying.
gloss.uat.text: 🙋 The people who asked for the work try it themselves and say whether it does what they need. AI-gile’s test pile is its version of this.
gloss.regression.text: ⏪ Something that used to work but broke after a change. Regression tests check that the old things still work.
gloss.smoke.text: 💨 A very quick check that the main things work at all, for example right after a change goes live. If it fails, stop and look.
gloss.exploratory.text: 🧭 Trying the product freely and poking at it in different ways, to find problems that planned checks would miss.
gloss.testcase.text: 📝 One written scenario to try: the steps, and what should happen.
gloss.coverage.text: ☂️ How much of the code is checked by automatic tests. More is usually safer, but high coverage alone doesn’t prove it works well.
gloss.testdata.text: 🎲 Made-up example information used while testing, so no real person’s private details are exposed.
gloss.edgecase.text: 🧗 An unusual situation at the limits, like an empty form or a name with an apostrophe, where things often break.
gloss.happypath.text: 😀 The normal route where everything goes right. Good testing also tries the unhappy paths 😢.
gloss.perftest.text: ⏱️ Checking how fast something is and how well it copes under strain.
gloss.loadtest.text: 🏋️ Checking how a system copes when lots of people use it at once.
gloss.sectest.text: 🔓 Looking for weaknesses that could let someone misuse a system or see what they shouldn’t.
gloss.accesstest.text: ♿ Checking that people with different abilities can use the product, including with a screen reader or only a keyboard.
gloss.linting.text: 🧽 An automatic check that spots likely mistakes and messy style in code, like a spelling checker for programs.
gloss.static.text: 👓 Checking code for problems by reading it automatically, without running it.
gloss.flaky.text: 🎰 A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails for no clear reason, so it can’t be fully trusted.
gloss.repro.text: 🔁 Making a bug happen again on purpose by following the same steps, so it can be studied and fixed. Writing those steps down is the most useful part of a bug report.
gloss.severity.text: 🌡️ How bad a problem’s effect is, from a small annoyance to everything stopping.
gloss.devops.text: ♾️ A way of working where the people who build software and the people who run it work as one team, with lots of automation, so changes go live often and safely.
gloss.cicd.text: 🔄 Everyone’s changes are joined into the main version often and checked automatically each time (continuous integration), so the software is always ready to go live at the press of a button (continuous delivery).
gloss.contdeploy.text: 🚀 One step further than continuous delivery: every change that passes the checks goes live by itself, with no button to press.
gloss.pipeline.text: 🚰 The automatic series of steps a change goes through on its way to live, like build, test, then deploy.
gloss.environment.text: 🏞️ One separate copy of the system for one purpose, such as one to build in, one to test in and the live one.
gloss.devenv.text: 🧑‍💻 The copy a developer works in, often on their own computer, where breaking things harms nobody.
gloss.testenv.text: 🧪 A separate copy of the system used just for testing, so the real service isn’t touched.
gloss.staging.text: 🎭 A last copy set up just like live, for a final check before a change goes live.
gloss.artifact.text: 📦 The file or bundle a build produces, ready to be stored, checked or put live.
gloss.hotfix.text: 🚑 An urgent fix put live quickly, outside the normal plan, because something important is broken.
gloss.patch.text: 🩹 A small update that fixes a bug or closes a security hole. Applying security patches quickly matters.
gloss.version.text: 🏷️ A label like 2.4.1 that says which release you have. Often the first number changes for big changes and the last for small fixes.
gloss.relnotes.text: 🗒️ A short plain list of what changed in a release, for the people who use it, including fixes and known limits. Also called a changelog.
gloss.flag.text: 🚩 An on and off switch for a feature, so new work can go live hidden and be turned on (or off again) without a new release.
gloss.rollfwd.text: ⏩ Fixing a bad release by quickly putting out a new, corrected version instead of going back to the old one.
gloss.canary.text: 🐤 Putting a change live for a small group first, and for everyone only once it looks fine. Named after the canaries miners took underground as an early warning.
gloss.bluegreen.text: 🔵🟢 Keeping two copies of the live system and switching people over to the new one in one go, so you can switch straight back if it goes wrong.
gloss.zerodown.text: 🟢 Putting a new version live without the service ever stopping for its users.
gloss.chgenable.text: 🧗 Helping changes succeed: weighing the risk ⚠️, getting the right approval and picking a good time. Also called change management.
gloss.cab.text: 🏛️ A group that looks over important changes and agrees whether and when they may go ahead.
gloss.stdchange.text: ✅ A low-risk change done the same tried and tested way each time, so it is approved in advance.
gloss.normchange.text: 📋 A change that needs to be checked and approved before it goes ahead.
gloss.emergchange.text: 🚨 A change that must happen right away to fix or prevent serious trouble, with a quicker approval to match.
gloss.automation.text: 🤖 Getting the computer to do a repeated job by itself, so it is quicker and done the same way every time.
gloss.infra.text: 🏗️ The machines, networks and services that software runs on.
gloss.iac.text: 📜 Describing your servers and settings in files kept with the code, so they can be rebuilt exactly the same way every time.
gloss.cloud.text: ☁️ Renting computers, storage and services from a big provider over the internet, instead of owning the machines yourself.
gloss.provider.text: 🏢 A company that rents out computing over the internet, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud.
gloss.hosting.text: 🏠 Where your app or website lives and runs so people can reach it, usually rented from a company.
gloss.domain.text: 🌐 The web address people type, like example.com. You rent it by the year 📅, so it must be renewed.
gloss.dns.text: 📖 Short for domain name system: the internet’s address book, which turns a name like example.com into the address of the right computer.
gloss.container.text: 🐳 A sealed package holding an app and everything it needs, so it runs the same on any computer. Docker is the best known tool.
gloss.vm.text: 🪆 A pretend computer running inside a real one, so one big machine can act as many.
gloss.serverless.text: 🪶 Running code without looking after any servers yourself: the provider runs it when needed and you pay for what you use.
gloss.lb.text: ⚖️ Something that spreads visitors across several servers, so no single one gets overwhelmed.
gloss.cache.text: 🧺 A handy store of recent results kept close by, so the same thing doesn’t have to be fetched or worked out again. Clearing it can fix pages that look out of date.
gloss.cdn.text: 🌍 A worldwide set of servers holding copies of your pages and pictures near your visitors, so they load quickly ⚡.
gloss.migration.text: 🚚 Moving data or systems from an old setup to a new one, or carefully changing how a database is laid out.
gloss.svcmgmt.text: 🛎️ Everything involved in keeping a service useful and working for the people who rely on it, day after day.
gloss.itil.text: 📘 A widely used guide to good service management, covering things like incidents, problems and changes. The name once stood for IT Infrastructure Library.
gloss.itsm.text: 🛎️ Running technology as a service for people, with clear ways to handle requests, incidents, changes and improvements.
gloss.managed.text: 🤝 A service someone else runs and looks after for you, under an agreement about how well it must work.
gloss.svcowner.text: 🧑‍💼 The person who answers for a service as a whole: how well it works, what it costs 💰 and how it improves.
gloss.sla.text: 📜 A written promise to customers about how well a service will work, like “up 99.9% of the time” or “answered within an hour”, often with money back if it is broken.
gloss.slo.text: 🎯 The team’s own target for how well a service should work over a period, usually set a bit stricter than the SLA to be safe.
gloss.sli.text: 📏 The actual measurement you check against a target, like the share of visits that loaded fine.
gloss.uptimepct.text: 🟢 How much of the time a service is working, usually as a percentage. 99.9% still allows about 43 minutes down a month.
gloss.availability.text: 🚪 Whether people can use a service when they need it, often measured as uptime.
gloss.downtime.text: 🔴 Time when a service isn’t working or is switched off, planned or not.
gloss.errorbudget.text: 🏦 The small amount of failure your reliability target allows. While some is left you can take risks with changes; once it is used up, you slow down.
gloss.outage.text: 💥 A time when a service is down or badly broken for its users.
gloss.degraded.text: 🐌 Working, but badly: slow, or with some parts not working.
gloss.monitoring.text: 👁️ Watching a service automatically all the time, so problems are spotted, ideally before users notice.
gloss.observability.text: 🔭 How well you can tell what is going on inside a system from the outside, using its logs, numbers and traces.
gloss.log.text: 📓 A running diary a program keeps of what it is doing, used to work out what went wrong.
gloss.trace.text: 🧵 A record of how one request travels through the different parts of a system, step by step, showing where it slowed down.
gloss.latency.text: ⏳ How long something takes to answer, like the wait between clicking and the page appearing.
gloss.alert.text: 🔔 An automatic message that something needs attention, like the website not answering.
gloss.alertfatigue.text: 😴 When there are so many alerts that people start ignoring them, including the important ones.
gloss.dashboard.text: 📊 A screen showing the most important numbers and statuses at a glance.
gloss.paging.text: 📟 Urgently calling or waking the on-call person about a problem.
gloss.escalation.text: 🪜 Bringing in someone with more skill or authority when an issue can’t be sorted at the current level, or not fast enough.
gloss.triage.text: 🏥 Quickly sorting incoming issues by how urgent and important they are, so the worst gets handled first.
gloss.impact.text: 💢 How much something affects people: how many, and how badly.
gloss.urgency.text: ⏰ How quickly something needs to be dealt with. Impact and urgency together set the priority.
gloss.plevels.text: 🚨 Labels for how urgent an issue is. P1 is the most serious and needs action straight away.
gloss.queue.text: 🚶‍♂️🚶‍♀️ The list of requests and incidents waiting to be picked up.
gloss.tiers.text: 🪜 Levels of support: first line takes the call and fixes simple things; second line has deeper skills for harder ones. Also called tier 1 and tier 2.
gloss.ic.text: 🎖️ The one person who leads the response to an incident, so everyone knows who decides and who does what.
gloss.responsetime.text: ⏱️ How long it takes before someone first picks up a request or incident.
gloss.resolution.text: ✅ How long it takes to fully sort out a request or incident, from report to fixed.
gloss.mttr.text: 🔧 On average, how long it takes to get a service working again after it breaks. MTTR can mean slightly different things, so say what you measure.
gloss.mtbf.text: ⏳ On average, how long a service runs before something breaks.
gloss.cmdb.text: 🗺️ The list of all your configuration items and how they connect, so you can see what depends on what.
gloss.asset.text: 💎 Anything of value you own or pay for to run the service, like a laptop 💻, a software licence or a domain.
gloss.capplan.text: 📐 Making sure there will be enough computer power, storage and people for what is coming.
gloss.scaling.text: 📈 Coping with more users by giving a machine more power (scaling up) or adding more machines (scaling out).
gloss.bcp.text: 🛟 Plans for keeping the important things going when something big goes wrong, like losing an office, a key supplier or the computers.
gloss.dr.text: 🌪️ The plan and tools for getting a service back after something serious, like losing a whole data centre.
gloss.rto.text: ⏱️ The longest a service may be down after a disaster before it must be working again.
gloss.rpo.text: 💾 How much recent data you could afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of one hour means backups at least every hour.
gloss.redundancy.text: 🛞 Having spares ready, like a second server, so one failure doesn’t stop the service.
gloss.failover.text: 🔀 Switching over to a spare system by itself when the usual one fails.
gloss.spof.text: 🧱 One part that takes everything down with it when it breaks, because there is no spare.
gloss.maintwin.text: 🔧 A planned time when a service may be paused or slow for upkeep, announced to users in advance.
gloss.handover.text: 🤝 Passing work, knowledge and responsibility to another person or team, so nothing gets dropped.
gloss.kb.text: 📚 A collection of help articles and answers, for users and for the team.
gloss.csat.text: 😊 A score from users saying how happy they were, often asked after a request is closed.
gloss.supplier.text: 📦 An outside company you rely on, like your hosting provider. Also called a vendor or third party.
gloss.retire.text: 🪦 Switching a service off for good, safely: telling its users, dealing with its data and access, and stopping its costs.
gloss.eol.text: 🌅 When a product stops getting updates or support from its maker, so it should be replaced.
gloss.cybersec.text: 🛡️ Protecting systems and data from being broken into, stolen or damaged.
gloss.authn.text: 🪪 Checking who someone is, usually with a password or a code. Often shortened to authn.
gloss.authz.text: 🎟️ Checking what someone is allowed to do once you know who they are. Often shortened to authz.
gloss.mfa.text: 📲 Logging in with two or more proofs, like a password plus a code on your phone. Also called two-factor (2FA).
gloss.sso.text: 🔑 Logging in once to get into many systems, like using your work account everywhere.
gloss.pwmgr.text: 🔐 An app that creates strong passwords and remembers them for you.
gloss.secret.text: 🤫 A password, key or other private code a program uses to get into something. It must never be shared or written into the code.
gloss.apikey.text: 🗝️ A secret code that lets a program use another service’s API, and shows who is using (and paying for 💰) it.
gloss.accesstoken.text: 🎫 A temporary pass that proves a program is allowed in, so it doesn’t need your password each time. Not the same as an 🤖 token.
gloss.encryption.text: 🔐 Scrambling information so only someone with the right key 🔑 can read it.
gloss.https.text: 🔒 The secure way web pages travel, shown by the padlock in your browser, so nobody in between can read or change them.
gloss.cert.text: 🪪 A digital ID card that lets a website prove who it is and use HTTPS. It expires ⌛, so it must be renewed.
gloss.permissions.text: 🚦 The rules for who may see or change what.
gloss.leastpriv.text: 🤏 Giving each person or program only the access they truly need, for only as long as they need it.
gloss.rbac.text: 🎭 Giving access by role, like viewer 👀 or editor ✏️, rather than person by person.
gloss.vuln.text: 🕳️ A weakness that someone could use to break in or cause harm.
gloss.zeroday.text: 0️⃣ A weakness attackers know about before the makers have had any time to fix it.
gloss.malware.text: 🦠 Harmful software, like viruses, made to damage, spy or steal.
gloss.ransomware.text: 🔒💰 Malware that locks up your files and demands money to unlock them. Good backups are the best defence.
gloss.phishing.text: 🎣 Fake messages that try to trick you into giving away passwords or money, or opening something harmful.
gloss.socialeng.text: 🎭 Tricking people, rather than computers, into giving access, like a fake call from “IT support”.
gloss.firewall.text: 🧱🔥 A guard that decides which network traffic may come in or go out.
gloss.vpn.text: 🕳️ Short for virtual private network: a private, scrambled link over the internet, often used to reach work systems safely.
gloss.ddos.text: 🌊 Flooding a service with so much fake traffic that real people can’t use it. DDoS means it comes from many computers at once.
gloss.pentest.text: 🥷 Hiring friendly experts to try to break in, so weaknesses are found before real attackers find them.
gloss.audit.text: 🔎 A careful check of how well something is protected, against a list of good practice.
gloss.threatmodel.text: 🗺️ Thinking through who might attack something, how, and what you would do to stop them.
gloss.breach.text: 🚨 When private information gets out to people who shouldn’t have it, or is lost or changed without permission.
gloss.pii.text: 🧑‍💼 Any information about a person who can be identified, like a name, email address or location. Also called PII.
gloss.gdpr.text: 🇪🇺 The European law on personal data (the UK has its own version): collect only what you need, keep it safe, and let people see or delete theirs.
gloss.dataprot.text: 🛡️ Looking after personal data properly and within the law.
gloss.privacypolicy.text: 📜 A public page saying what personal data you collect, why, and what you do with it.
gloss.consent.text: 👍 A person’s clear, free yes to their data being used in a particular way. They can take it back at any time.
gloss.cookie.text: 🍪 A small file a website saves in your browser to remember things, like being logged in. Some need your consent first.
gloss.minimisation.text: 🤏 Collecting and keeping only the personal data you really need for the job.
gloss.retention.text: 🗓️ How long data is kept before it is deleted 🗑️. Keeping it no longer than needed is safer and often the law.
gloss.anon.text: 🫥 Changing data so nobody can reasonably be identified from it any more.
gloss.pseudo.text: 🎭 Swapping names and other details for codes, with a key kept apart to link them back. It is still personal data.
gloss.dpa.text: 📝 A contract saying how a supplier may handle personal data on your behalf.
gloss.dpia.text: 🔍 A careful look, before you start, at how a plan to use personal data could affect people and how to lower the risks.
gloss.auditlog.text: 📒 A record of who did what and when, so actions can be checked later.
gloss.compliance.text: ✅ Following the laws, rules and standards that apply to you, and being able to show that you do.
gloss.iso.text: 🌐 A well known international standard for managing information security. Companies can be certified against it.
gloss.soc.text: 🇺🇸 A US report, checked by outside auditors, showing a company looks after customer data properly.
gloss.ai.text: 🤖 Computer systems that do things we usually think need a person, like writing ✍️, answering questions ❓ or recognising pictures 🖼️.
gloss.ml.text: 🧠 A way of making computers learn patterns from lots of examples, instead of giving them exact rules.
gloss.model.text: 🧠 The trained “brain” of an AI system, built by learning from huge numbers of examples. Models differ in skill, speed ⚡ and price 💰.
gloss.llm.text: 📚 An AI model trained on vast amounts of text, so it can read and write language.
gloss.genai.text: 🎨 AI that creates new things, like text, pictures or code, rather than only sorting or spotting them.
gloss.chatbot.text: 💬 A program you talk with in everyday language, by typing or speaking.
gloss.prompt.text: ⌨️ What you give an AI: your question or instructions, plus anything you hand it. Clearer prompts usually get better answers.
gloss.prompteng.text: 🪄 The skill of writing prompts that get reliable, useful results.
gloss.sysprompt.text: 📜 Background instructions an AI gets before the conversation starts, setting its role and rules. They weigh more than what you type.
gloss.context.text: 👀 Everything the AI can see while it works: the instructions, your messages, files it has read and earlier replies.
gloss.ctxwin.text: 🪟 How much an AI can keep in mind at once, measured in tokens. Past that, older parts get dropped or summarised.
gloss.session.text: 💬 One working conversation with an AI, from start to finish. A new session starts with a fresh memory.
gloss.memory.text: 📓 Notes an AI keeps between sessions, so it remembers your preferences and past decisions.
gloss.hallucination.text: 🌈 When an AI says something that sounds sure of itself but is made up or wrong. Check important facts.
gloss.training.text: 🏋️ Teaching a model by showing it huge numbers of examples, before anyone uses it.
gloss.trainingdata.text: 📚 The examples a model learned from. Its knowledge stops at the date that data was collected.
gloss.cutoff.text: 📅 The date an AI’s built-in knowledge ends. It won’t know about later things unless it looks them up.
gloss.finetune.text: 🎛️ Extra training of an existing model on your own examples, to make it better at one particular job.
gloss.inference.text: 💡 An AI model actually being used to answer something, as opposed to being trained.
gloss.tooluse.text: 🛠️ An AI being able to do things, not just talk: run commands, read files or search the web, through tools the app gives it.
gloss.subagent.text: 🤖➡️🤖 A helper AI that a main AI hands a smaller job to, and gets the result back from.
gloss.multiagent.text: 🤖🤖🤖 Several AIs working together on one piece of work, each with its own part, like a small team.
gloss.autonomy.text: 🦅 How much an AI may do on its own before it has to ask a person.
gloss.hitl.text: 🧑‍⚖️ Keeping a person involved to check or approve what the AI does at key points. In AI-gile that is you.
gloss.guardrails.text: 🚧 Limits and checks that keep an AI’s actions safe, like needing approval before anything goes live. They lower the risk of mistakes, but don’t rule them out.
gloss.rag.text: 📖 Letting an AI look things up in your own documents before it answers, so its answers rest on your facts.
gloss.embedding.text: 🔢 Turning text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so a computer can find things that mean similar things.
gloss.vectordb.text: 🗄️ A database built to search those lists of numbers (embeddings), to find material with a similar meaning.
gloss.mcp.text: 🔌 A common way to plug tools and data sources into AI apps, so an AI can use them.
gloss.temperature.text: 🌡️ A setting for how adventurous an AI’s answers are. Low gives steadier, more predictable answers; high gives more varied ones. Neither makes it always right.
gloss.multimodal.text: 🎞️ Able to work with more than one kind of information, such as text 📝, pictures 🖼️ and sound 🔊.
gloss.evals.text: 🧪 A planned test of how well an AI does on chosen examples, so you can compare models or prompts.
gloss.bias.text: ⚖️ When an AI (or a person) leans unfairly one way, often because of what it learned from.
gloss.responsible.text: 🌍 Using AI fairly, safely and honestly, with people still answerable for the results.
gloss.injection.text: 💉 A trick where hidden instructions in a web page or file try to make an AI do something its user didn’t ask for.
gloss.ratelimit.text: 🚏 A cap on how many requests you may send to a service in a set time. Go over it and you have to wait ⏳.
gloss.usagelimit.text: ⚡ How much AI work your plan allows in a period, after which it pauses or costs more 💰.
gloss.vibe.text: 🎵 Building software mostly by describing what you want to an AI and letting it write the code.
gloss.budget.text: 💰 The amount of money set aside for something.
gloss.costest.text: 🧮 A best guess at what something will cost before you start.
gloss.roi.text: 📈 What you get back compared with what you put in. If it is positive, it was worth it.
gloss.tco.text: 🧾 Everything something really costs over its whole life, not just the price to buy it: running, support, upgrades and finally retiring it.
gloss.capex.text: 🏦 CapEx is money spent up front on things you keep; OpEx is ongoing spending, like monthly bills.
gloss.subscription.text: 🔄 Paying regularly, usually monthly or yearly, to keep using something.
gloss.saas.text: ☁️ Software you use online and pay for by subscription, while the maker runs it for you.
gloss.payg.text: 🚰 Paying only for what you use, like cloud computing or AI tokens.
gloss.overage.text: 📈 Use above what your plan includes, which can cost extra 💸.
gloss.billingalert.text: 🔔 A message when spending or use reaches a level you chose. It warns you, but doesn’t always stop further charges.
gloss.freetier.text: 🆓 A free level of a paid service, with limits. Handy for starting out.
gloss.pricing.text: 🏷️ The different packages a service sells, each with its own price and limits.
gloss.licence.text: 📜 The rules for how you may use, copy, change or share something someone else made, such as software, fonts or pictures.
gloss.opensource.text: 🔓 Software whose code anyone can read, use and often change for free, under the rules of its licence.
gloss.osslicence.text: 📜 The rules that come with open source code. Some let you do almost anything (like MIT); some ask you to share your changes too (like GPL).
gloss.proprietary.text: 🔒 Owned by a company and not free to copy or change. The opposite of open source.
gloss.copyright.text: ©️ The legal right of a creator to control copies of their work, including code and writing.
gloss.ip.text: 💡 Ideas and creations the law treats as owned, like code, designs, names and logos.
gloss.tos.text: 📃 The rules you agree to when you use a service.
gloss.contract.text: 🖊️ A written agreement between two sides that the law will back up.
gloss.sow.text: 📑 A document setting out exactly what work will be done, by when and for how much.
gloss.fixedprice.text: 🏷️ An agreed price for the whole job, however long it takes.
gloss.tm.text: ⏱️💰 Paying for the hours really worked and the things really used, rather than a set price.
gloss.invoice.text: 🧾 A bill asking for payment for work done or goods supplied.
gloss.lockin.text: ⛓️ When moving away from a supplier is so hard or costly that you are stuck with them.
gloss.procurement.text: 🛒 The process of choosing and buying from suppliers.
gloss.servicecredit.text: 💸 Money back or a discount you get when a supplier misses its SLA.

gloss.ci.text: One thing your service depends on, like a server 🖥️, a domain, a certificate 📜, a key or a supplier. 🗂️ Configuration items lists them per service, so you can see what an incident 🔥 affects and what needs renewing or a backup.
gloss.expiry.text: ⌛ The date something stops working unless it is renewed, like a website’s security certificate or its web address. AI-gile watches these dates and makes one card to renew each one 30 days before, so nothing stops by surprise.

gloss.svcrequest.text: Someone asking for something ordinary, like a new account or a bit of help, rather than reporting that something is broken 💥. It waits its turn; an incident 🔥 goes first.

gloss.accessreview.text: 🔑 Checking every 90 days who can still get in: share links, friends’ roles and saved passwords and keys. You keep or remove each one, so old access doesn’t linger.
gloss.improvements.text: Everything the team 👥 decided to get better at, in one place: retro suggestions, review actions and problem 🧩 fixes 🔧, each with its status. Find it under 📈 Improvements.
gloss.tokencap.text: A monthly limit on the tokens 🪙 a service’s agents 🤖 may use. At 80% you get a warning; at 100% their background work waits until next month 📅 or until you raise the cap.

guide.inc.hi:
- An **incident** 🔥 is a card 🃏 for "it is broken now". It jumps the queue and has a red 🔴 edge.
- Closing it asks three short questions ❓: what happened, why, what we change.
- If the same thing breaks again, group 👥 the incidents 🔥 under one **problem** 🧩 with its root cause and a workaround.
- The real fix 🔧 goes through a change request.
guide.inc.steps:
1. Raise the incident: **New card**, type **🔥 incident**.
2. Fix 🔧 it first. Use the workaround if the problem 🧩 card has one.
3. Move it to done. Fill in **What happened**, **Why**, **What we change**, then **Done**.
4. It happened before? Ask your lead to group 👥 the incidents 🔥 under a **🧩 problem** card (the commands are under *For agents*).
5. The problem 🧩 card 🃏 shows the **Root cause**, the **Workaround**, the incidents and the change request.
6. Later incidents 🔥 join the same problem 🧩; the card lists them all.
7. Raise a change request for the fix 🔧. The problem 🧩 stays open until that change is done.
guide.inc.full:
- **Why it matters:** an incident 🔥 is about getting back to normal fast. A problem 🧩 is about the cause. Mixing them means you fix the same fire again and again.
- **Incident:** the post-mortem has no blame 🙅. It says what happened, why, and what changes so it does not repeat. A risk from the risk register that happens files an incident 🔥 for you.
- **Problem:** one cause, many incidents 🔥. Root cause is the reason behind the reason (not "the server was down" but "the deploy script skips the tests"). The workaround is what anyone does until the fix 🔧 ships.
- **Linking:** an incident 🔥 belongs to one problem 🧩. Linking shows on both cards. Linking it to another problem moves it.
- **Change request:** the fix 🔧 is a change like any other, with a reason, a risk and a way back. The problem 🧩 stays open until that change is done.
- **Good habits:** look at open problems 🧩 in each retro; if three incidents 🔥 share a cause, make the problem; keep workarounds short enough to follow while stressed.
guide.inc.agents:
- Raise an incident: `aigile add <proj> "Site is down" --type incident`
- Make a problem: `aigile problem <proj> add "Deploys break the site" --incidents AIG-1,AIG-2`
- Cause and workaround: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 --cause "..." --workaround "..."`
- Link a later incident: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 link AIG-12`
- Link the change request: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 --change AIG-20`
guide.svc.hi:
- Tell the board 📋 which projects are **services**: what they offer, who uses them and their web address. The board then watches the address for you.
- When a service 🛎️ stops answering, the board 📋 raises **one incident** by itself. A card that waits too long shows a red ⏰ "reply by" clock.
- A really bad incident 🔥 gets the **🚨 Major** button: one click wakes the right agent and tells you. A public status page shows friends 🤝 what is up.
- What you learn is kept: **🧩 Known errors**, **📖 Runbooks** (how to fix 🔧 X) and a **📝 Post-incident review** on each major incident 🔥.
- Keep an eye on the **🗂️ Items** your service 🛎️ stands on (expiry dates, backups 💾), the **🔐 Access review** every 90 days, **🚀 Releases**, the **📈 Improvements** list and, once a month, the **📆 Review** (with an optional monthly token cap).
guide.svc.steps:
1. On the project board 📋 click **🎨 Look**. In the **Project settings** dialog find the **🛎️ Service** section. Tick **This project is a service** and fill in what it offers, who uses it and its web address.
2. Choose the **On-call agent** (the lead 🧭 by default) and tick **Public** if friends 🤝 may see it on the status page. Optionally type a **Monthly token cap** so one project cannot eat the whole budget. Click **Save**.
3. Look at the project's dot on **Home**: green means the address answers. If it stops answering, an incident 🔥 card 🃏 appears by itself.
4. Open that incident 🔥 card 🃏. A bad one? Click **🚨 Major**. Click **End major incident** when it is over.
5. Cards 🃏 that wait too long show a red ⏰. Open them first. The inbox filter **Desk: incidents** shows only incidents 🔥 from friends and the feedback form.
6. Click **⋯ More** on the board 📋, then **🗂️ Items**. Click **+ Add item** for each server 🖥️, domain, certificate, key, repo or supplier. Add an expiry date and, for data, where it is backed up and how often. Click **Backed up today** after each backup.
7. On an incident 🔥 card 🃏, look at the **📖 Runbooks** box: it lists the how-to notes that match. Click **Open** to read one.
8. After a major incident 🔥 is done, its card 🃏 shows **📝 Post-incident review**. Read the timeline, then click **Make a card** next to each thing worth changing.
9. Click **⋯ More**, then **🧩 Known errors** to see problems that have a workaround. Click **🚀 Releases**, type a name like v1.3 and click **🚀 New release** to gather the done cards 🃏 into notes. **↩ Roll back** files an undo checklist card.
10. Click **⋯ More**, then **📆 Review** once a month 📅: use **← Earlier** and **Later →** to change month, and **✍️ Summary** for a two-line summary from the on-call 📞 agent.
11. Click **⋯ More**, then **📈 Improvements** (also in the **❓ Help** menu) to see retro ideas, review actions and problem 🧩 fixes 🔧 in one list. In **Setup**, click **Run access review now** to see who can get in, then **Keep** or **Remove** each one.
guide.svc.full:
- **Service details:** in **🎨 Look**, **Project settings**, **🛎️ Service** you say what a project offers, to whom, at what web address and who is on call 📞. Only projects you tick count as services.
- **Uptime dot:** every few minutes ⏱️ the board asks the web address if it is alive. Green is fine; red means it did not answer. Three misses in a row open one incident 🔥, never a pile, and a comment says when it was back ("Up again after N min").
- **Reply-by ⏰:** each kind of card has a time to reply by (an incident 🔥 about an hour, a friend 🤝 request a couple of days, a bug about a week). Late cards go red and the daily brief lists them. These are aims, not promises.
- **🚨 Major:** for an incident 🔥 that hurts many users or risks money or data. One click turns on the swarm, wakes the on-call 📞 agent, sends you one note and asks for a "Status:" comment every 30 minutes.
- **Status page:** a public page shows each public service as green, orange or red with the latest status line. It never shows card 🃏 text, only the line you or the agent 🤖 chose.
- **Service desk:** reports from friends 🤝 and the feedback form are sorted into **Request**, **Incident** or **Idea**. The inbox filter (**Desk: all**, **Desk: requests** and so on) shows one kind. A report that looks like a card 🃏 you already have says "looks like AIG-12" with a **Link** button.
- **🧩 Known errors:** a problem with a known cause and a workaround that is not done yet. They are listed per project and for all projects, and go into each agent's brief, so nobody investigates twice.
- **📖 Runbooks:** short step-by-step notes on how to fix 🔧 a thing. An incident 🔥 card shows the ones that match its title. After a review, the agent can propose a new runbook and you say Go or Not yet.
- **📝 Post-incident review:** after a major incident 🔥 is done, the agent 🤖 writes a **Timeline**, **What helped** and **What to change**. Each action becomes a card with **Make a card**. If no agent is free, you write it yourself.
- **🗂️ Items:** the list 📝 of things a service 🛎️ stands on, with a **Kind** (server, domain, certificate, key, repo, supplier, other). Each can have links to cards or web addresses. A key is only its name from Secrets, never the key itself. Incident and change cards can show what they **Affect**.
- **Expiry and backups:** each day the board checks expiry dates and backup 💾 age. A card appears before something runs out or when a backup is too old, and once a month 📅 a restore-test card reminds you that a backup you never tried to restore is only a hope.
- **Server health:** the board watches CPU, memory and disk on your servers 🖥️ and raises an upgrade card 🃏 before they fill up.
- **🔐 Access review:** every 90 days one card lists share links 🔗, friends' roles and kept secrets 🤫 (names only), each with **Keep** or **Remove**. Run it now from **Setup**.
- **🚀 Releases:** a release is a named bundle of the cards 🃏 that became done since the last one, with short notes. **↩ Roll back** files a checklist card with the undo steps.
- **📈 Improvements:** retro suggestions, review actions and problem 🧩 fixes 🔧 in one list, filterable by project, so good ideas do not get lost between retros.
- **📆 Monthly review:** one page per service for one month: incidents 🔥 opened and closed, average time to fix, cards that met their reply-by target, uptime, tokens used and server 🖥️ peaks. Open it from **⋯ More → 📆 Review** or from **Project settings → Service**.
- **Monthly token cap:** in **Project settings → Service** you can set a monthly limit of tokens 🪙. At 80% the daily brief warns you; at 100% background runs for that project wait until next month 📅 or until you raise the cap. Your own Wake still works.
- **Good habits:** fill in the service details first, keep the web address correct, look at the status dot daily, write up every major incident 🔥 and check the improvements list after each retro, and read the monthly review while the month 📅 is fresh.
guide.svc.agents:
- Raise an incident: `aigile add <proj> "Site is down" --type incident`
- Problem cause and workaround: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 --cause "..." --workaround "..."`
- Configuration items: `aigile ci <proj>` lists them; `aigile ci <proj> add <kind> <name>` adds one
- Runbooks: `aigile runbook <proj>` lists them; `aigile runbook <proj> <name>` prints one
- Major incident (owner or lead): `aigile major <proj> <incident id> --as NAME`; run it again to end it
- Post-incident review: `aigile pir <proj> <incident id> --timeline ".." --helped ".." --actions "one | two" --as NAME`
- Runbook from a review: `aigile pir-runbook <proj> <incident id> <name> --text ".." --as NAME`
- Releases: `aigile release <proj>` lists; `aigile release <proj> <name> --as NAME` makes one; add `rollback` to undo it
guide.msg.hi:
- **💬 Messages**, at the top of the left rail, holds all your chats: project leads, friends 🤝, agent groups 👥 and each project's Meeting Room. The filters **🤖 Agents**, **🙋 People** and **🎥 Meeting Rooms** show one kind.
- A **DM** is a private chat with one lead 🧭 or one friend 🤝. Chats with friends are encrypted on the way and on this computer.
- A **group** puts two or more agents 🤖 in one chat 💬: write once and each of them answers.
- In a friend's chat 💬, **📞 Call** starts a voice or video call, with **🖥️ Share screen**. Each project's Meeting Room has its own **🎥 Join call**.
- Mic 🎤 or camera 📷 blocked? Allow it in the browser's address bar. You can always still listen.
guide.msg.steps:
1. Click **💬 Messages** at the top of the left rail. Pick a filter to see only **🤖 Agents**, **🙋 People** or **🎥 Meeting Rooms**.
2. Click a project's lead 🧭 to talk to that team directly. Type and press Enter; the lead answers in the same chat 💬.
3. Click a friend 🤝 under **🙋 People** to chat 💬 with them. A friend shows up here once they have joined with your invite.
4. To ask several agents 🤖 at once, click **＋ New group**, give it a name, tick two or more agents and click **Create**.
5. In a friend's chat 💬 click **📞 Call**. Your friend 🤝 sees that you are calling and clicks to join. Use **🔇 Mute**, **📷 Camera on** and **🖥️ Share screen**, and **Leave call** when you are done.
6. Under **🎥 Meeting Rooms**, open a project's room to talk to its whole team 👥 in one chat 💬. Click **🎥 Join call** for its voice or video call.
7. The first time, the browser 🌐 asks for the microphone 🎤: click **Allow**. Said no by mistake? Click the icon at the start of the address bar, allow the microphone and call again.
guide.msg.full:
- **One place for every chat:** **💬 Messages** lists leads, friends 🤝, groups 👥 and Meeting Rooms together, newest first. The filters only change what you see; nothing is moved or deleted.
- **Leads:** every project has a lead. Their chat is the quickest way to ask that team something without making a card. Each answer is an agent 🤖 run, so it uses tokens 🪙.
- **Friends:** a friend 🤝 runs their own AI-gile. Your DMs go between your two boards, encrypted, and are kept encrypted on this computer too. Replies, reactions and typing dots work like any chat 💬 app.
- **Groups:** you and two or more agents, from any project. Each message you write wakes each member once to reply, so a big group 👥 uses more tokens 🪙.
- **Meeting Rooms:** one per project, with the agents on its team as members, always up to date. The call 📞 in a Meeting Room is for you only: friends 🤝 and agents cannot join it.
- **Calls:** voice and video calls 📞 work out of the box through AI-gile's own call server 🖥️, for you and for your friend; nothing to set up. To use your own LiveKit server, open **Setup → Calls → Advanced**.
- **Screen share:** in a call 📞 click **🖥️ Share screen**; the browser 🌐 asks which screen, window or tab. Click **🖥️ Stop sharing** to stop.
- **Microphone, camera and speaker:** the call 📞 panel has a chooser for each, handy with a headset or a second camera 📷.
- **When the mic or camera will not work:** "blocked" means the browser 🌐 said no: allow it in the address bar. "Not found" means nothing is plugged in or switched on. "In use by another app" means another call 📞 app has it: close that one. You can always still listen.
- **A call that drops:** you see "Reconnecting…" first. If it ends, check your internet 📶 and call 📞 again.
- **Good habits:** use a group 👥 or a Meeting Room for a question to several agents instead of copying it, mute when you are not talking, and share one window rather than the whole screen 🖥️.
